title: Z-Algorithm
tagline: For each position, the length of the longest prefix match — linear-time matching and periodicity.

intuition.analogy: Standing at each character and asking 'how far from here do I keep agreeing with the very start of the string?'. Crucially, when you're inside a region you've already compared, you can reuse those comparisons instead of redoing them.
paragraphs: The Z-array gives, for each index i, the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. It solves pattern matching by forming P + separator + T and scanning for Z-values equal to |P|.

The trick to linear time is the [l, r] 'Z-box' — the rightmost segment known to match the prefix. Inside it you can copy a previously computed Z-value (mirroring), only extending past r with actual comparisons. Each character is compared O(1) amortised times.
It's an alternative to KMP that many find more intuitive, and it directly answers periodicity and border questions.
intuition.keyIdea: Maintain the rightmost prefix-matching window [l, r]; reuse mirror values inside it, extend only beyond r.

steps.title: Initialise
steps.detail: z[0] is conventionally 0 (or n). Keep a window [l, r] of the rightmost match to the prefix, initially empty.

steps.title: Reuse inside the box
steps.detail: If i ≤ r, start z[i] = min(r − i + 1, z[i − l]) — mirror the value from the prefix.

steps.title: Extend and update
steps.detail: Extend z[i] by direct comparison past r; if i + z[i] − 1 > r, update [l, r] = [i, i + z[i] − 1].

complexity.timeReason: The right boundary r only moves forward, bounding total comparisons by n.

pitfalls: Use a separator not in the alphabet when concatenating pattern and text.
min(r − i, z[i − l]) vs (r − i + 1) — boundary conventions differ; be consistent.
z[0] is a special case (the whole string matches itself).

dryRun.clickMoment: z[4]=3 reveals that the suffix starting at index 4 re-runs the prefix 'aab'. Detecting that overlap is exactly what powers fast matching and periodicity tests.
